about: T19 captions, written as a warm tutor speaking; each line starts at film time t (seconds). Can be recorded as voiceover later.

lines.text: Lesson nineteen, and the start of Phase 5: scalping and risk management.
First question: what is scalping?
So far you've learned to read candles, timeframes, trends, zones and volume.
Now: how do short-term traders use them? And what does it really cost?
Let's look honestly, costs and all.
Scalping means trying to profit from small price moves, in trades that last minutes.
Sometimes only seconds. Then the trader exits and waits for the next one.
Think of a stall that makes many small sales, each with a thin margin.
Thin margins mean costs matter a lot.
Here's a fictional 15-minute chart of 1-minute candles.
A scalper might notice two things. These are observations, not signals.
One: price dips to a support zone and holds. Two: a sudden spike on thin volume.
Say a demo long opens at 60,000 and closes 4 minutes later at 60,120.
Held for 4 minutes. Price move: +120 USDT. It could have failed.
Now the costs. The position is 0.1 BTC: 6,000 USDT at 60,000.
Gross profit: 0.1 × 120 = 12.00 USDT.
Fees at an example 0.05% each side: 3.00 to enter, 3.01 to exit.
Net: 12.00 − 3.00 − 3.01 = 5.99 USDT. Half the move went to fees.
A losing scalp pays fees too, so the loss gets bigger.
Trade frequency is how many trades you make in a period.
Each round trip here costs about 6 USDT in fees.
Twenty trades in a day: about 120 USDT in fees, win or lose.
And every trade is one more chance to be wrong.
More trades is not more profit.
Execution quality is how close your fill is to the price you expected.
Say you slip 10 USDT getting in and 10 getting out.
Our 120 move shrinks to 100, before fees.
When moves are small, spread and slippage take a big share.
How does scalping compare with holding for days or weeks?
Scalping: minutes, many trades, costs are a big share of each small move.
Longer holding: fewer trades, bigger moves, but more time exposed to news.
Neither is safe. Both can lose money.
A note on XORA. It looks at about 10 to 15 minutes of recent price for context.
That is an analysis horizon. It is not a time you must hold a trade.
And it is not a promise of where price will be in 15 minutes.
Some moments are simply not good for trading.
Very thin markets. Wild news spikes. Fees bigger than the expected move.
No clear reason, no stop, or you're tired, upset or chasing a loss.
In all of these, NO_TRADE is the right call. Waiting is a skill.
Your turn. A scalp's expected move is 60 USDT per BTC, at a price of 60,000.
Round-trip fees are 0.10%. Is it worth taking? Pause and think.
Fees: 60,000 × 0.10% = 60 USDT per BTC. The move only covers the fees.
Even before slippage, it's zero. NO_TRADE makes sense.
Before you try scalping, even in demo, know the limits.
It is not easy money. Many small losses and fees add up fast.
Fast decisions bring mistakes, and leverage makes every loss bigger.
Practise in demo first. NO_TRADE is always allowed.
Let's recap.
Scalping aims for small moves in short trades: seconds to minutes.
Fees, spread and slippage take a big share of small moves.
XORA's 10 to 15 minutes is context, not a holding rule. NO_TRADE is allowed.
Check yourself: a move of 60 USDT per BTC, fees of 60. Worth it?
No. It only covers fees, before slippage. Waiting is the better call.
Well done! Next up: evaluating an entry opportunity. See you in lesson twenty.
